releases.title: Faster, more accurate usage engine

highlights.title: Costs are priced from the vendor, not whichever reseller sorted first
highlights.description: Pricing picked the alphabetically first provider publishing a model, so resellers beat the vendors who make them. gpt-5.6-luna was billed at $1.00/$6.00 instead of OpenAI's $0.20/$1.20 — a 5x overcharge that hid an 80% price cut. Measured against models.dev, 18% of models with a known first-party price were wrong, from 0.05x to 267x. Providers are now ranked so the vendor always wins.

highlights.title: Prices are dated, so a cut no longer reprices your history
highlights.description: Rates carry the date they took effect and a call is priced at the rate in force when it happened, instead of every past session being silently repriced by today's snapshot. Long-context surcharges, per-provider cache-write rates and the batch tier's 50% discount are all applied too.

highlights.title: Repeated calls are no longer counted twice
highlights.description: Resuming, forking or compacting a session copies earlier messages into the new transcript. Half of all Claude assistant messages on the test machine were such copies, and Codex forks replayed an entire parent conversation into each child. Both are now detected and counted once, which cut one day's reported Codex spend from $3,790 to $119.

highlights.title: Unknown models are reported as unpriced instead of guessed
highlights.description: A model with no rate on file used to fall back to $2/$10 per million tokens, which billed 965 sessions of a free model $380. Unpriced usage is now excluded from the total and called out, so the headline figure only contains money we can actually account for.

releases.title: DeepSeek Harness support

highlights.title: DeepSeek Harness (dsh) sessions are tracked
highlights.description: TokenTelemetry now discovers DeepSeek Harness sessions from their local logs, showing tokens, cost, and model/provider per session (DSH is multi-provider, so a session can mix a free local Ollama model with a paid cloud one and each part is priced correctly). Subagent sessions DSH spawns are linked back to the session that started them.

releases.title: Install fixes for Linux, faster setup with uv

highlights.title: Installs no longer stop at "No module named pip"
highlights.description: On Debian and Ubuntu, Python creates the virtual environment but leaves pip out of it unless the separate python3-venv package is installed, so the first launch failed on the backend dependencies. The launcher now bootstraps pip itself, and if that isn't possible it names the package to install instead of showing a pip traceback. Thanks to yannschepens for reporting this (issue #267).

highlights.title: Setup uses uv when you already have it
highlights.description: If uv is on your PATH, first-run setup uses it for the virtual environment and the dependency install: about 0.4 seconds instead of 2.8 on a warm cache, with the same Python and the same hash-checked packages. Nothing to install and nothing to configure; without uv the setup works exactly as before.

releases.title: Filter the step index on a session trace

highlights.title: Narrow a long trace to the steps you care about
highlights.description: The Step Index on a session trace now has a filter next to its heading, listing every event category in the session with a count: user prompts, responses, reasoning, and each tool by name. Tick the ones you want and both the index and the trace beside it drop to just those steps, which makes a run with several thousand steps navigable. Thanks to hwantage for building and contributing this (PR #269).

releases.title: Hermes session explorer keeps your place

highlights.title: Load more, and filters that stay put
highlights.description: The Hermes session explorer grows the list with a Load more button instead of walking page by page, and the footer says how many of the matching sessions are on screen. Filtering, moving to another page and coming back now returns you to the same filtered list, and the filters stay in the address bar so a filtered view is still something you can bookmark or share.

releases.title: Muse Code and Prime Agent support

highlights.title: Muse Code and Prime sessions are tracked
highlights.description: TokenTelemetry now discovers Muse Code and Prime Agent sessions from their local logs, grouping them by project and showing their traces, models, token usage, costs, and available subagent or branch details.

highlights.title: Agent brands are easier to scan
highlights.description: Connected agents, settings, project badges, trace headers, and the website now use each agent's own mark and color so mixed-agent work is easier to recognize at a glance.

releases.title: Find any Hermes session without loading them all

highlights.title: Hermes session explorer
highlights.description: The Hermes dashboard now keeps the overview compact and links to a dedicated session explorer. Search, filter by project, source, or model, sort by time, cost, or tokens, and move through the history 50 sessions at a time.

highlights.title: Cleaner Codex trace timelines
highlights.description: Codex traces now collapse mirrored messages and repeated reasoning snapshots, so the Step Index and conversation show each visible turn once instead of replaying the rollout's internal projections.

releases.title: Hermes telemetry that says what it doesn't know

highlights.title: Latency recovered from rotated logs
highlights.description: TokenTelemetry only ever read ~/.hermes/logs/agent.log, so once Hermes rotated that file, per-call latency silently disappeared. On a real install that meant none of 22 sessions showed any timing, while 14 sessions' worth sat unread in agent.log.1. Rotated logs are now parsed too, oldest first, and sessions with no timing anywhere say "not captured" instead of showing zero.

highlights.title: Every cost says where the number came from
highlights.description: A Hermes dollar figure can come from four places: reported by Hermes, estimated by Hermes, priced by TokenTelemetry, or not priced at all. They used to render identically. Each figure now carries its source, sessions that could not be priced read "not captured" rather than $0.00, and a local or subscription-covered run is labelled "no marginal cost" instead of being shown as a $0.00 price.

highlights.title: Completion and failure rates by source and model
highlights.description: Hermes records why each session ended, but only three of its end reasons were ever displayed, so on a real install 9 of 22 sessions showed no outcome at all. Every end reason now maps to one of seven outcomes, broken down per source and per model. An end reason TokenTelemetry does not recognise appears by name as unknown rather than being counted as a completion.

highlights.title: Tool reliability
highlights.description: Tool failures were already parsed out of the Hermes log and then discarded. The Hermes page now shows which tools are used most and which fail most, counting only tools with at least three calls so a single failed call does not read as a 100% failure rate.

releases.title: See what /goal runs actually cost

highlights.title: Goal cards on the session trace
highlights.description: Sessions where you set a goal now show a Goal Mode card. Codex reports the objective, status, tokens and time itself. Claude Code shows how many times the goal blocked the agent from stopping and the extra tokens those turns cost. Grok shows its progress checkpoints, and Antigravity shows the goal you typed. An unattended overnight run is no longer indistinguishable from an ordinary session.

highlights.title: Every goal says where its status came from
highlights.description: Only Codex records real goal status, so only Codex cards show it as fact. Everything else is marked "inferred", and a Claude goal is never shown as finished because Claude writes no completion event. The card would rather say "unknown" than guess.

highlights.title: Goal cost is never double-counted
highlights.description: Cost means three different things here, and each card says which. Codex tokens are shown as a share of the session that already contains them, Claude shows only the extra turns a blocked stop caused, and Grok and Antigravity say plainly that the session is the goal.

releases.title: Run TokenTelemetry in Docker or Podman

highlights.title: Container support via Docker or Podman
highlights.description: TokenTelemetry now ships Dockerfiles and a Compose file, so you can run it as a container instead of installing Python and Node on the host. A Makefile handles the rest: `make up` builds and starts, `make down` stops, `make logs` tails output, auto-detecting whether you have Docker or Podman. The dashboard serves on port 13000 and the API on 18000, both loopback-only, and your agent logs are mounted read-only. Thanks to slmingol for building and contributing this (PR #172).

highlights.title: Pre-built images, no local build
highlights.description: Multi-arch images (Intel and Apple Silicon) are published to GitHub Container Registry, so `make up-prod` pulls and runs without compiling anything. Pin a specific build with `TT_IMAGE_TAG=sha-abc1234` when you want a known-good version.

releases.title: Active loops now show their next run

highlights.title: Next run time on active loops
highlights.description: Every loop that's still live now shows when it fires next — in the Recurring loops list on Analytics, on each loop card in a project's Config tab, and in the loop card on the session trace. Heartbeat loops project from the last fire and cadence; cron loops compute the next real match of their schedule. Overdue-but-alive loops read "due now" instead of hiding the field.

highlights.title: Truer cancelled vs expired loop states
highlights.description: A loop is no longer marked cancelled just because its session deleted some other scheduled task. Claude cron deletes now count only when they name the loop's own job id, and Grok deletes only when they happened after the loop's last firing — so still-running loops keep their real state.

releases.title: Agent artifacts, per project

highlights.title: Claude Code published artifacts
highlights.description: When Claude Code publishes an artifact (a hosted claude.ai page), TokenTelemetry now finds it in the session transcript and shows it: each project workspace gets an Artifacts tab listing every published page with its title, description and link, and the session inspector shows the pages published in that session. Publishes made from git worktrees roll up to the main repo's card.

highlights.title: Antigravity artifacts too
highlights.description: Google Antigravity's own artifacts — the task list, implementation plan and walkthrough it writes per session — appear on the same Artifacts tab, with the summary and updated time from Antigravity's metadata. Internal (non-user-facing) docs are left out.

highlights.title: Artifact previews and a list view
highlights.description: Cards on the Artifacts tab now preview the artifact itself: a scaled-down render of the page's local HTML source for Claude publishes (while the file still exists — nothing is fetched from the internet), and an expandable markdown preview for Antigravity docs. A Cards/List toggle switches to a compact row view; your choice is remembered.

releases.title: See the reasoning effort each session ran at

highlights.title: Reasoning effort across agents
highlights.description: A session's context panel now shows the model reasoning effort it actually ran at — for every agent that records one: Claude, Codex, Copilot, Grok, Hermes and Pi (values like minimal / low / medium / high / xhigh, or Pi's off). When the effort changed mid-session, the progression is shown (e.g. "medium → xhigh") instead of a single value. Agents that don't record a discrete effort setting simply don't show the row.

releases.title: See which experimental features each agent has on

highlights.title: Agent feature flags in Settings
highlights.description: Settings now shows the experimental and preview features each coding agent has enabled in its own local config — at a glance whether Copilot's experimental mode (the one that unlocks /every and /loop), Codex's per-feature flags, or Claude Code's feature toggles are on or off, plus the exact command and a docs link to turn each on in the agent itself. It's read-only and local-first; agents that gate features server-side aren't listed rather than faked.

releases.title: See which sessions ran a loop

highlights.title: Loop badge on every session trace
highlights.description: When a session scheduled a recurring or self-paced prompt (a /loop, a cron, or a self-perpetuating agent), its trace header now shows a Loop badge with the live state: active, expired, or cancelled. Open any past session to see which loop ran, its cadence and job id, and why it ended.

highlights.title: Recurring loops in Analytics
highlights.description: A new Recurring loops section counts your active, expired and cancelled loops with their observed fire counts, cadence and cost, so a forgotten hourly loop quietly burning tokens is easy to spot. It's detected from the actual scheduling calls, so it catches loops even when the /loop command left no trace.

highlights.title: Per-project loop view
highlights.description: Open any project and its Config tab now lists every recurring loop set up there — state, cadence, fire count and job id — so you can see at a glance which automations are still running in that repo. The Insights tab adds the numbers: active/expired/cancelled counts and the token & cost footprint of the loops' own fire turns, scoped to that project.

highlights.title: Loops from other agents, not just Claude
highlights.description: Recurring loops set up in Grok Build (its `/loop` scheduler / Grok Tasks) and Cline (Scheduled Agents) are now detected too — each schedule's cadence, fire count and cancelled/expired state show up in the trace and the loop views alongside Claude's, tagged with the agent that ran it. Where an agent reports only a whole-session token total (Grok) or fires each run as its own session (Cline), the loop shows cadence and fires with cost marked n/a rather than a made-up number.

releases.title: Compare two Hermes profiles head-to-head

highlights.title: Profile diff view
highlights.description: Pick any two profiles and see them side by side: sessions, tokens, cost, 7-day burn and unattended spend as mirrored bars, daily cost paired on one scale, and each profile's top models. Thanks to mvinca-bandwidth for requesting profile cost comparison (issue #142).

releases.title: Hermes profiles: burn, budgets & swarm costs

highlights.title: Filter the Hermes dashboard by profile
highlights.description: A profile switcher scopes every stat, model and session list to one profile (or all, grouped with each profile's color — the same color Hermes desktop gives it). Spot at a glance which persona a session belongs to.

highlights.title: Know which profile is burning budget
highlights.description: Each profile card now shows a 14-day cost sparkline, 7-day burn with trend, and how much of it was spent unattended (cron, subagents, kanban workers). Set an alerts-only monthly budget per profile right on the card — the overnight-swarm surprise bill gets caught early.

highlights.title: Kanban swarm board with per-task cost
highlights.description: Hermes tracks swarm tasks but never prices them. The new Kanban page shows every board's tasks by status with the cost of each task's linked session, per-worker cost lanes, and failure/retry burn.

releases.title: Hermes profiles: per-profile usage

highlights.title: See which Hermes profile spent what
highlights.description: If you run multiple Hermes profiles (work, personal, per-client), Hermes itself has no combined view of their usage. The Profiles page now shows every profile with its sessions, tokens, cost, last activity, gateway status, skills and cron jobs — and each session is tagged with the profile that ran it.

highlights.title: Profile sessions get their full trace details
highlights.description: Session timings, per-call latency and working-directory info for sessions run under a named profile were silently missing (only the default home's logs were read). Profile logs are now picked up, so those sessions show the same detail as everything else.

releases.title: Pi Coding Agent support

highlights.title: Pi sessions now show up automatically
highlights.description: If you use the Pi Coding Agent, its sessions are now detected and tracked alongside Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and the rest — grouped by project, with the full prompt/response trace, tools used, and model. Nothing to configure; TokenTelemetry reads Pi's local session history. Thanks to Tharun-tharun for requesting this (issue #135).

highlights.title: Accurate per-turn cost, including local models
highlights.description: Pi records real token usage on every turn, so cost is computed per message using that turn's own model — mixed-model sessions add up correctly. When Pi runs against Ollama or another local endpoint, those turns are priced by electricity instead of API rates.

releases.title: Every session tracked, correctly dated

highlights.title: Full session history — not just the last 100
highlights.description: Claude Code and Codex used to stop tracking real usage once you passed 100 sessions; anything older sat frozen as a blank, zero-token row. Every session is now fully scanned, with a local cache keeping repeat scans fast, so your full history — and its true token/cost totals — stays accurate no matter how many sessions you've run. Thanks to mariadb-KyleHutchinson for reporting and fixing this (PR #131).

highlights.title: Reopening an old session no longer misdates it
highlights.description: Opening an old Claude session (e.g. from VS Code's history sidebar) used to bump its reported date to today, scattering old work into the wrong day on Analytics and sometimes tripping a false "recent activity" alert. Sessions are now dated by when the conversation actually happened.

releases.title: Readable session intents & per-step tokens

highlights.title: IDE sessions now show your actual prompt
highlights.description: Sessions started from the VS Code or JetBrains Claude plugins used to show "No prompt content" or raw editor tags in the sessions list. The list now skips the editor context and shows the first words you actually typed, so you can find the right session at a glance.

highlights.title: Token usage on every step of a trace
highlights.description: Open a session trace and each step now shows the tokens that API call used — a small chip under the step and a per-step count in the step index. Makes it easy to scan an expensive session and spot which step was the main offender.

releases.title: Git worktrees, grouped under their project

highlights.title: Worktrees roll up to the parent repo
highlights.description: Work split across git worktrees used to scatter into separate, disconnected project cards with split totals. Each repo now links to its worktrees and shows combined metrics, with a per-worktree breakdown — including deleted worktrees — that adds up to the whole.

releases.title: Set spend budgets, get alerted at 80% & 100%

highlights.title: Per-project & per-agent spend budgets
highlights.description: Set a monthly, weekly, or rolling-30-day limit (in dollars or tokens) on any project, and optionally per agent. It's observational — TokenTelemetry never blocks an agent — so it just tracks this period's spend against your limit: a colour-coded pill on the project header and a per-agent breakdown on the Insights tab.

highlights.title: Alerts when you cross your thresholds
highlights.description: Each budget raises an alert when spend passes 80% and 100% of the limit (thresholds are configurable). Alerts collect in a new notification center — the bell at the bottom of the sidebar — and surface once as a banner, so you learn you're over without watching the dashboard.

releases.title: See an agent's files right in its trace

highlights.title: Antigravity session artifacts now show in the Artifacts tab
highlights.description: Open an Antigravity session and the files it produced are right there in the trace's Artifacts tab — its markdown audit/QA reports render formatted (with their embedded screenshots inline) and every captured screenshot appears as a thumbnail. Click any artifact, or the new expand icon, to open it full-screen, and download any file in one click. No more digging through ~/.gemini to find what a run created.

releases.title: Privacy you can see — and switch off

highlights.title: Anonymous usage stats, explained plainly
highlights.description: As TokenTelemetry evolves we need to understand how it's actually used — which features deliver value — so we can make it better for everyone. The app now shares a small set of anonymous usage signals: which pages and features you use, your OS and app version, and a coarse country derived at the network edge (never your IP). It carries nothing about your work — no code, prompts, file paths, project names, tokens, or costs. It's on by default so the picture is representative, but one click turns it off under Settings → Usage & privacy, and DO_NOT_TRACK=1 (or TT_NO_TELEMETRY=1) forces it off for restricted or enterprise environments.

releases.title: Analytics by date — and history that survives cleanup

highlights.title: Filter analytics by date range, week, or month
highlights.description: The graph is no longer stuck at the last 7 days. Pick a preset (7d, 30d, this month, this year), set a custom range, or switch the buckets to weekly/monthly — and narrow to specific agents or models. Everything is filtered server-side, so even a full year stays fast.

highlights.title: Your history no longer disappears when agents prune it
highlights.description: Coding agents quietly delete their own session transcripts on a schedule (Claude Code after 30 days by default), which used to erase your older analytics with them. TokenTelemetry now keeps a tiny durable summary of every session it sees, so long-range trends survive. Under Settings you can see each agent's cleanup window, opt to keep full transcripts past it, and reclaim space anytime without losing your stats.

releases.title: Truer costs: local power + which credit pool pays

highlights.title: Local-model power cost now reads your actual chip
highlights.description: Self-hosted models are priced by electricity, and the default wattage now comes from your detected chip (e.g. an Apple M-series part) instead of a one-size-fits-all 80 W. On machines we can't auto-detect, the field stops pretending and asks you to enter your draw under load (or click Measure) — so the estimate is honest rather than a silent placeholder.

highlights.title: See which credit pool each agent actually drains
highlights.description: Providers no longer bill an agent through one bucket. Expand any agent under Settings to see its drain order, split by interactive vs programmatic use — including Claude's separate Agent-SDK credit pool (claude -p, SDK, CI) that has no auto-fallback, plus pool sizes and stops-at-$0 warnings. Pick your plan tier to size the pools. It explains the cost framing; it doesn't change the math.

releases.title: See what your subagents, skills & MCPs cost

highlights.title: Subagent spend, finally visible
highlights.description: When a Claude Code session spawns subagents (Explore, general-purpose, custom agents), their tokens were invisible until now — on a typical machine that's millions of tokens. Session pages show a "Delegated work" card with each subagent's task, model, tokens and cost, priced by the model the subagent actually ran (an Explore on Haiku no longer hides inside an Opus session).

highlights.title: Which subagent types earn their keep
highlights.description: Analytics gains a Delegation & ecosystem section: total delegated tokens and cost, plus a per-type ranking. If general-purpose agents cost you 5× what Explore agents do for similar work, you'll see it — and can change how you delegate.

highlights.title: Skill & MCP usage, cross-linked to your inventory
highlights.description: Sessions now record which skills you invoked and how often each MCP server was actually called. Your project's Config page overlays that usage on every installed skill, command, subagent and MCP server — anything marked "no recorded use" is a candidate to clean up.

highlights.title: Delegation across Grok Build, Codex & Antigravity too
highlights.description: Grok Build, Codex and Antigravity CLI all spawn subagents as separate sessions — those are now linked: the parent session shows each spawn (task, duration, role) with a jump to the child session, and children link back to their parent. Cursor shows spawn counts; agents that don't log spawns say so honestly instead of showing a misleading 0.

highlights.title: Recent Codex sessions were missing — now found
highlights.description: Newer Codex versions stopped updating the session index TokenTelemetry relied on, so sessions from the last weeks never appeared. Sessions are now discovered from the session files themselves — expect your Codex session count (and totals) to jump to reality.

releases.title: View the dashboard from another device

highlights.title: Opt-in remote / tailnet access
highlights.description: Run TokenTelemetry on a headless box (a home server, a Tailscale tailnet) and open the dashboard from your laptop or phone. Start it with --host 0.0.0.0 and --allowed-origins <your-hosts>; the frontend now figures out where the backend is from the address you loaded it on, so the same setup works over localhost, a LAN IP, or a tailnet name. Default is unchanged: localhost-only.

highlights.title: Protected by an access token
highlights.description: Exposing the dashboard puts your data on the network, so remote access now requires a token: when you start with a non-loopback --host, a random token is printed once in the server console — enter it on the other device when prompted. Your own browser on the server is exempt, and a fully trusted private network can opt out with --insecure-no-auth.

highlights.title: Scan to connect — no typing
highlights.description: When remote access is on, Settings shows a "Connect a device" panel with a QR code. Scan it from your phone or tablet and the dashboard opens already signed in — the token rides along in the link, gets stored on the device, and is cleared from the address bar automatically.

releases.title: Store your data wherever you want

highlights.title: Choose where TokenTelemetry keeps its data
highlights.description: Config and state no longer have to live in ~/.tokentelemetry on your system drive. Launch with --data-dir /your/path (or set TOKENTELEMETRY_DATA_DIR) and everything — aliases, hidden projects, preferences, billing/power overrides, the summaries cache — moves together to that folder. Handy for keeping your main drive clear or putting app data on a secondary disk.

releases.title: Local model insights: energy, savings & CO₂

highlights.title: Dedicated Local & Power insights surface
highlights.description: A new dashboard card brings your local model usage front and center — total local energy (Wh/kWh), estimated cloud savings from running locally, and a breakdown of which local models you use most.

highlights.title: Energy consumption insights
highlights.description: TokenTelemetry now estimates the energy consumed (in Watt-hours) for local generation based on your actual hardware's power configuration and model throughput.

highlights.title: Savings vs. cloud estimates
highlights.description: See how much you save by running locally: TokenTelemetry compares your local generation cost against a configurable reference cloud model (default Claude Sonnet) so you can track your API savings.

highlights.title: Carbon footprint estimate
highlights.description: Set your grid's carbon intensity alongside your power rate, and TokenTelemetry tracks the CO₂ grams generated by your local AI sessions based on real hardware draw and session duration.

releases.title: Real cost for the local models you run

highlights.title: Local models priced by your actual hardware
highlights.description: Sessions on Ollama, llama.cpp or vLLM are now detected by their endpoint/provider — not by guessing — so a local model is always costed by electricity, never at cloud API rates (even when it shares a name with a cloud model). Generation time uses each model's real throughput where measurable (a 4B isn't costed like a 70B).

highlights.title: Set or measure your machine's power
highlights.description: A new Settings → Local power & electricity card lets you set your watts-under-load and kWh rate, mark local/LAN and flat-subscription endpoints, and — where your OS allows it without admin — measure real power draw directly. The estimate is honest about where its numbers come from.

releases.title: More accurate cost estimates

highlights.title: 2000+ models priced for accurate cost estimates
highlights.description: Cost estimates now draw on a much larger, regularly-refreshed pricing dataset (sourced from models.dev), so far more models — and provider-specific rates — get an accurate price instead of a generic fallback. The data ships with each update and is read entirely on your machine: no new outbound calls, same local-first privacy.

highlights.title: Local models priced by electricity, not fake API rates
highlights.description: Models you run yourself (Ollama, llama.cpp, vLLM) have no API bill — their real cost is power. Set your machine's watts under load and your kWh rate, and TokenTelemetry estimates the electricity cost instead of inventing a per-token charge.

highlights.title: Flat subscriptions now show $0 per call
highlights.description: Endpoints you pay for monthly (Ollama Cloud Pro, a proxied gateway) are billed by subscription, not per token. List them as subscription endpoints and their sessions stop inflating your per-call cost totals.

highlights.title: Full subscription-cost disclaimer
highlights.description: The dashboard's "API equiv. (est.)" figure used to cut off mid-sentence at "Subscription users p…". The disclaimer now shows in full, plus a persistent callout makes clear the number re-prices your usage at API list rates for comparing sessions — it is not an invoice. On a flat-fee plan like Claude Pro/Max or Copilot, your actual spend is much lower.

highlights.title: Per-agent billing mode — bill vs. estimate, framed right
highlights.description: If you pay per token (API key) for an agent, the cost figure approximates your real bill; on a flat subscription it's only an API-list-price equivalent. TokenTelemetry now auto-detects which one you're on per agent (from each agent's own auth — e.g. ~/.codex/auth.json) and frames the number accordingly, with a Settings → Billing & cost control to override any agent.

releases.title: Update check — now visible and yours to control

highlights.title: Check-for-updates toggle
highlights.description: TokenTelemetry's one outbound call — an optional check that tells you when new features ship — now has a switch in Settings → Updates & privacy. It sends no usage data; turn it off any time, or set TT_NO_UPDATE_CHECK=1 to enforce it off.

highlights.title: Clearer privacy wording
highlights.description: Docs and site now state precisely what stays local (all your logs, sessions, tokens, and costs) and what the update check does, so the privacy promise matches the behavior.

releases.title: Antigravity CLI — real model & accurate projects

highlights.title: Real model for Antigravity CLI sessions
highlights.description: Sessions from the Antigravity CLI (agy) now show the actual model they ran (e.g. "Gemini 3.1 Pro (High)") instead of a generic "gemini (antigravity)" label, read straight from each session's own trajectory.

highlights.title: Accurate, stable project for Antigravity CLI sessions
highlights.description: CLI sessions are now grouped under the exact folder they worked in, read from each session's own saved record — so the grouping stays correct over time instead of guessing from task text. Sessions that genuinely never entered a project (pure chat/research) stay grouped separately, off the Projects view.

releases.title: Summarize with any OpenAI-compatible server

highlights.title: OpenAI-compatible summarizer backend
highlights.description: Point TokenTelemetry at any server speaking the OpenAI /v1/chat/completions API — llama.cpp, vLLM, LM Studio, LocalAI, or Ollama's OpenAI endpoint — to generate trace summaries. No extra CLI to install: set the endpoint, model, and (optionally) an API key, tune sampling, and hit Test connection.

releases.title: Antigravity — tokens, IDE coverage, surface labels

highlights.title: Antigravity token usage
highlights.description: Antigravity sessions now show estimated token usage instead of zero, read from the session transcripts.

highlights.title: Antigravity IDE sessions tracked
highlights.description: Sessions from the Antigravity IDE (not just the CLI) are now picked up, and overlapping sessions are de-duplicated so counts stay accurate.

highlights.title: Antigravity surface sub-label
highlights.description: Antigravity sessions carry a small CLI / IDE / APP tag so you can tell which surface a session came from. They still roll up under one Antigravity total.

releases.title: GitHub Copilot CLI support

highlights.title: GitHub Copilot CLI sessions tracked
highlights.description: TokenTelemetry now reads GitHub Copilot CLI / agent sessions from ~/.copilot/session-state, so your terminal Copilot usage shows up alongside everything else — model, tokens, project, and full trace.

highlights.title: Copilot surface sub-label
highlights.description: Copilot sessions now carry a small CLI or VS Code tag so you can tell at a glance which surface a session came from. They still roll up under one Copilot total.

releases.title: Grok Build support + tracking fixes

highlights.title: Grok Build (xAI) support
highlights.description: TokenTelemetry now tracks xAI's Grok Build coding agent — sessions, context usage, tool calls, permission decisions, and plan mode — with a dedicated forensics card. That's 11 agents tracked in total.

highlights.title: GitHub Copilot tracking restored
highlights.description: Recent VS Code versions changed how Copilot chats are stored on disk, which made new sessions read as zero. TokenTelemetry now reads the new format, so your recent Copilot sessions show up again.

highlights.title: Smarter 'Back' from a session
highlights.description: Opening a session and hitting Back now returns you to the page you came from — e.g. the project you were viewing — instead of always jumping to the dashboard.

releases.title: Summarizer + ports + update banner

highlights.title: Summarizer settings
highlights.description: Pick a backend (Ollama / Codex / Claude / Gemini / Qwen / Antigravity) and choose a specific model for it. Avoids 'incorrect API key' errors when your account doesn't have GPT-5, or 'timed out' when Ollama's default model is too big for your hardware.

highlights.title: Configurable ports
highlights.description: start.sh now accepts --port (frontend) and --api-port (backend), e.g. start.sh --port 4000 --api-port 9000. The frontend is told the backend's location automatically via NEXT_PUBLIC_API_BASE, so fetches always reach the right place.

releases.title: Hermes sub-pages

highlights.title: Hermes Agent dashboard
highlights.description: New sub-pages for Gateway, Memory, Profiles, Schedules, Skills, Soul, and Tools — all read directly from your local ~/.hermes state.
